{{nihongo|'''Sugihokowake no Mikoto Shrine'''|杉桙別命神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Izu Province]].

[[File:Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, otorii.jpg|thumb|250px|right|{{center|Otorii}}]]'''Sugihokowake no Mikoto Shrine'' is located in {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in Tanaka. In {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}}, {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=Old company rank}} is {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|qid=Q134917316}}. '''Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine'' (not ``Kawazu'') <ref>[https://sugihokowakenomikoto.jimdo.com/ Official site of Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine (Sugisawabetsu no Mikoto Shrine)]</ref><ref>[http://www.kawazu-onsen.com/sightseeing/25 Large camphor tree of Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine] - Kawazu Town Tourism Association</ref>.

It is in charge of '''{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Himemiya Shrine}}''', which is compared to ``Sasahara Hime no Mikoto Shrine'', a Shikinai shrine.

=== Company name ===
In ancient times, it was called ``Sawabetsu Myojin'', ``Kino (Great) Myojin'', ``Kinomiya (Great) Myojin'', ``Kino Shrine'', ``Kino Shrine'', and ``Kinosaki Myojin'', and even today it is commonly known as ``Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine''. It is said to be a shrine with {{ill|Kinomiya Faith|Q11296898|qid=Q11296898}}, as it has passed down the ancient name of ``Kinomiya'' and ``Tori Shojin Sake Shojin'' (described later).

=== Enshrined God ===
The main deity is ``Sugihokowake no Mikoto'', and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Isotake no Mikoto}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sukuhikona no Mikoto}} are enshrined in {{ill|Aidono|Q135009883|qid=Q135009883}}. In "{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}", it is listed as 1 dai, so it is thought that it was originally dedicated to Sugisubetsu no Mikoto. </ref>.

=== History ===According to the shrine's legend, it had been enshrined since ancient times, but was rebuilt in the {{ill|Wadō (era)|Q1373026|qid=Q1373026}} period (708 - 15), and was listed as a small shrine in the Engishiki Shinmyocho. In addition, in the shrine biography, in {{ill|Kenkyū|Q1193933|qid=Q1193933}}4 ({{ill|1193|Q19741|qid=Q19741}}), {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800}} rebuilt it and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sharyo}}93{{ill|Koku|Q855048|qid=Q855048|lt=stone}} was dedicated, and the shrine building was further rebuilt by {{ill|Kujō Yoritsune|Q471780|qid=Q471780}} in {{ill|1226|Q5405|qid=Q5405}}. In {{ill|Kōei|Q980266|qid=Q980266}} 2nd year ({{ill|1343|Q6072|qid=Q6072}}), {{ill|Izumi Province Divine Name Register|Q11420490|qid=Q11420490}}, ``{{ill|Izu Province Shinto Name Book|Q17193087|qid=Q17193087}},'' it is written as ``Junior Fourth Rank Upper, Hokowake no Myojin.'' According to the shrine's legend, the shrine was rebuilt by Yoshitane Ashikaga|Q708527} in {{ill|Eishō (Muromachi period)|Q1193577|qid=Q1193577}}10 ({{ill|1513|Q6200|qid=Q6200}}), and 12 families served {{ill|Shake (social class)|Q11588367|qid=Q11588367}}. (era name)|Q1192853|Tenbun}} In the 7th year ({{ill|1538|Q6470|qid=Q6470}}), the shrine and other buildings were completely destroyed by fire, and in the 13th year of the same year ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=1544}}), after the shrine's territory was washed away by a flood, it fell into disrepair and was enshrined in a small shrine, but it is said that the governor of the country {{ill|Shimizu Yasuhide|Q11560955|qid=Q11560955}} and others rebuilt it.In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}}6 ({{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}}), he was appointed to Gosha. {{ill|Post-war|Q1201472|qid=Q1201472}} belongs to {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}. Furthermore, the Shinto priest has been served by the {{ill|Kawazu clan|Q11553993|qid=Q11553993}} for generations.

=== Precincts ===

=== Shrine building ===
The main shrine was rebuilt in {{ill|Kashō|Q1373157|qid=Q1373157}}2 ({{ill|1819|Q6967|qid=Q6967}}), and is {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}}. The roof is {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=copper plate roof}} with {{ill|Bargeboard|Q4881511|qid=Q4881511|lt=staggered gable}} and eaves {{ill|Bargeboard|Q4881511|qid=Q4881511|lt=kara gable}}.

=== Big Kusu of Sugisubetsu no Mikoto Shrine ===
[[File:Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, okusu-1.jpg|thumb|250px|{{center|[[Big Kusu of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja|Big Kusu]] (National Natural Monument)}}]]
{{Main|Big Kusu of Sugisubetsu no Mikoto Shrine}}
A {{ill|Camphora officinarum|Q158722|qid=Q158722|lt=camphor}} with a tree height of about 24m and a trunk circumference of 14m. The tree was estimated to be over 1,000 years old in the early {{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} period (first half of the 20th century), and was designated as a national {{ill|Natural monument|Q23790|qid=Q23790}} in 1936|Q18649}}. Since ancient times, it has been called ``Kimiya-sama's great Kusu'' and has been worshiped as {{ill|Shinboku|Q48743901|qid=Q48743901}}. There were once seven large camphor trees in Kawazu, and until the mid-Meiji period they were called ``Nanaka Kae Nanakusu,'' but this is the only one that remains today. There is also a large camphor tree near the approach entrance and in front of the shrine to the right.

In addition, there is also {{ill|Kinomiya Shrine|Q11523682|qid=Q11523682}} in {{ill|Atami|Q653364|qid=Q653364}} in the northern part of {{ill|Izu Peninsula|Q822822|qid=Q822822}}. alink|Azu Sawaki Shrine's Large Kusu|Q60403026}} There is a famous camphor tree (also a natural monument), which is often called the same name as "Kimiya Shrine's Kusu", so it is easy to confuse it.

=== Festival ===
Sakeru Festival (December 17th) / Sake Festival (December 24th) - Between the two festivals (December 18th - 23rd) is called {{ill|Kawazu's Tori Shojin Sake Shojin|Q11553983|qid=Q11553983}}, and it is said that when Sugisabetsu no Mikoto, who was drunk in the area, was about to burn to death in a wild fire, he was saved thanks to a large flock of small birds carrying water from their wings and extinguishing the fire, so Sugisabetsu no Mikoto forbade him to drink alcohol and eat poultry and eggs.

=== Company name ===
In ancient times, it was called ``Himemiya'' or ``Himemiya Daimyojin.''

=== Enshrined God ===
Wakamiya Hachiman Shrine ({{jalink|Emperor Nintoku|Q3 13119|Osazaki no Mikoto) and Kageyama Shrine (Kageyama Myojin) were enshrined together<ref>Properly, it was enshrined at Wakamiya Hachiman Shrine, and the main deity was changed to Sasahara Hime no Mikoto. </ref>.

=== History ===
Ritual artifacts thought to date back to the 4th century have been unearthed near the former shrine grounds (305 Sasahara Himamiya, Kawazu-machi, currently on the grounds of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kawazu Town Minami Elementary School}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Himemiya Kindergarten}}) ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Himemiya Ruins}}), and it appears that it has been worshiped as a {{ill|Ubusunagami|Q1392097|qid=Q1392097}} since ancient times. It is listed as a small shrine in the ``Engishiki Shinmyocho'', and is described as ``Junior Fourth Rank Upper Sawarahime no Miko'' in the ``Izu Province Shinto Namecho''. According to the shrine's biography, the shrine had territory until around {{ill|Genki (era)|Q1145064|qid=Q1145064}} (1570 - 73), but for the {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}} years (1573 - It is said that it was confiscated in 1992), and in {{ill|Bunroku|Q1373039|qid=Q1373039}}5 ({{ill|1596|Q6785|qid=Q6785}}), a company official called Tosho took away the old records and declined. It was rebuilt by the people of the entire Kawazu village in {{ill|Kanbun (era)|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228}} 4th year ({{ill|1664|Q7581|qid=Q7581}}), and was listed in {{ill|Son-sha|Q134917284|qid=Q134917284}} in 1896, In 1213, Wakamiya Hachiman Shrine, which was located at the current site (slightly northeast of the current site), was enshrined together with the nearby Kageyama Shrine, and the company name was changed to ``Himemiya Shrine'' and the main deity was changed to ``Sasahara Hime no Mikoto''. - It was rebuilt in 2019). </ref>, In 1962, it was moved to the side of the main shrine of Sugisubetsu no Mikoto Shrine, but it was moved again in {{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}}14 ({{ill|2002|Q1987|qid=Q1987}}).

=== Shrine building ===
The main shrine is one-span {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}} on both the front and sides, with a {{ill|Wood shingle|Q199388|qid=Q199388}} roof with a staggered gable and a kara gable on the eaves. It is a late {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}} shrine building.
